summary: Narrow verification of revision 10 of the knee-edge OOD draft: the two user-decided rule changes, the r9 must-fix resolutions, and a whole-document consistency sweep; skeptics; readiness critic

packed.verdict:
Both user decisions are implemented correctly, and I found no new false-PASS, false-FAIL or wrong-reading path. No gate, label, precedence or approval rule changed beyond decisions (a) and (b).

Decision (a): per anchor, KC_C - min(KC_R,0) >= KC_C - KC_R, so the counterfactual median is never below K1a. Withholding reading 2 whenever that counterfactual reaches +0.5 covers every FAIL that needed RANDOM's positive KC, by definition. It also implies median KC_C alone < 0.5, so the reviewers' second suggested guard adds nothing. Reading 2 can therefore never be attached to a FAIL RANDOM caused.

The cost is over-withholding. The counterfactual keeps RANDOM's negative KC, so zero-mean RANDOM noise can withhold the reading when CUTOFF's own median is below the bar. In simulation this happens 22% of the time at sigma_R = 0.1 with a CUTOFF median of 0.45, and 61% at sigma_R = 0.2. This is conservative (the label stays FAIL), but the prose blames it on kink rounding.

Decision (b): I checked the dominance proof analytically and by 20,000-case brute force with zero violations. Dropping minus-infinity entries never lowers a median, so M >= 0.65. Per-anchor dominance plus a constant shift gives a C-valid median KC >= M - 0.15 >= 0.5M. The absolute clause stays on the common anchors, at most 10% of anchors are non-C-valid, and C-validity does not depend on the critic's outputs. So the change opens no meaningful false-PASS path.

Every example number recomputes exactly: the 47-anchor case, the 48-anchor companion case and the 48-anchor K1c case (1.40 vs 0.70, alternative bar 0.33). Decision (c) is recorded accurately as a cost to power only.

What is left is wording and disclosure:
- 'in every seed' is missing from two restatements of condition (b).
- The noise routing points only to K1a's joint statement, not to K1c.
- The step 0.4 forecast counts invalid anchors differently from Stage 1.
- The 4.8 batching change is a method change, though not a rule change.
- The over-withholding of reading 2 is undisclosed.

r10 is ready for A1 consideration after an optional text-only touch-up.

low_findings.section: Part 5 reading 2 (lines 714-717); Part 2 line 219; Part 8.2(iii) lines 873-874

The text then blames RANDOM's kink rounding for the withholding. The rule is conservative, but the stated reason is not always the cause.
low_findings.evidence: Per anchor, KC_C - min(KC_R,0) >= KC_C >= ... and cf >= median KC_C. Deterministic case: 48 anchors, KC_C = 0.45 everywhere, KC_R = -0.1 at 24 and +0.1 at 24. Median KC_R = 0, condition (a) passes, K1a = 0.45, median KC_C = 0.45 (fails with RANDOM exact), cf = 0.50, so reading 2 is withheld. Simulation (scratch verify_wf_r10/rules/checks.py; 48 anchors, KC_C ~ m + N(0,0.1), KC_R ~ N(0,sigma_R)), P(withheld | K1a fail and median KC_C < 0.5): 0.22 at sigma_R=0.1, m=0.45; 0.61 at sigma_R=0.2, m=0.45; 0.70 to 0.93 at m=0.48. A cf >= 0.5 can also be carried by RANDOM's negative KC at low-gap anchors, the same mechanism 8.2(iv) warns about. Reading 2 line 717 says 'Otherwise RANDOM's own kink rounding could explain the miss'.
low_findings.fix: Disclosure only, without reversing the decision. Add one line to 8.2(iii): '(b) keeps RANDOM's negative KC, so it is conservative: a withheld reading does not by itself show that RANDOM's positive KC caused the miss. With zero-mean RANDOM noise, reading 2 can be withheld when median KC_s05(CUTOFF) alone is just under 0.5. Read it together with the median-KC_s05(CUTOFF) companion.' checked_ok: The 47-anchor reading-2 example recomputes exactly: gate (i) 0.9, gate (ii) 0.9, median KC_R 0, K1a 0.45, K1a with positive KC_R zeroed 0.90. All anchors are valid and 47 >= 32, so V0(c) and item 5 are satisfied (scratch checks.py).
The 48-anchor 8.2(iv) example recomputes exactly: gates 0.60 and 0.60, median KC_R 0, smooth K1a 0.70, low-gap share 23/25 = 0.92, median KC_C 0.70.

The 48-anchor K1c example recomputes exactly: gate 0.66 (passes 0.65); C-valid median rho_hat 1.40 and bar 0.70; r10 C-valid KC median 1.40; r9 common KC median 0.66; alternative bar 0.33; absolute clause 0.66. The worst-case smooth critic (KC = rho_hat - 0.15) gives absolute 0.51 and relative 1.25 >= 0.70.

The dominance proof is valid. Removing the k smallest (minus-infinity) entries never lowers a median, under both odd and even averaging. Per-anchor KC >= rho_hat - 0.15 gives median KC >= median(rho_hat) - 0.15, because a median is monotone under per-anchor dominance and commutes with a constant shift. M - 0.15 >= 0.5M iff M >= 0.3. A 20,000-case brute force over 32-48 anchors with up to 10% non-C-valid found 0 violations of either K1c clause.

Condition (b) never attaches reading 2 to a FAIL that needed RANDOM's positive KC. cf >= K1a per anchor, so cf < 0.5 is exactly 'K1a fails without positive KC_R'. cf < 0.5 also implies median KC_C alone < 0.5, which covers the reviewers' second suggested guard.
Condition (b)'s strict '< +0.5' matches K1a's '>= +0.5' pass rule. It uses the same common gated anchor set and the same s05 slot as K1a.

'In every seed' for (b) matches reading 2's precondition: a reading applies only when K1a fails in all seeds, and (b) must hold in all seeds. Part 2 line 219, reading 2 and the per-seed consistency check agree.
Readings precede no label: (b) changes only whether reading 2 is attached, and label precedence (5.0 table) is unchanged.

The K1c rule is stated identically in Part 2 line 226, the anchor-set bullet line 655 and the Part 5 table row line 686. V0(d)'s 'K1c is reachable' (line 672) is unchanged and is now sufficient for both clauses.
C-validity depends on predictor fit to simulated Q_nostall, not on the critic's Q at the anchor, so the C-valid restriction does not select on the critic's outcome.

V0(c)'s 32-anchor C-valid floor and item 5's 90% keep the relative clause's medians over at least 32 anchors, and over at least 90% of the common set. The absolute clause stays on the common set, which bounds any leniency from dropping non-C-valid anchors.
Reading 1's 'with the s10 gap shown reachable (V0(d))' is now accurate for both K1c clauses. In r9 it held only for the absolute clause.

Part 2 'What a K1a miss means' (lines 216-217): a miss by a smoothly extrapolating CUTOFF critic implies a gate failure by dominance, so it is INCONCLUSIVE, consistent with the new definition of 'extrapolates smoothly'.

Decision (c) is recorded accurately at line 875 and in Review 10: the drafted scoping is kept, and the cost is power only, because masked outcomes are recorded per seed (5.0) and labelled INCONCLUSIVE by the existing precedence.

The diff touches only the declared hunks. V0(d) clauses (i), (ii) and the K1c gate, the K1a row, the label precedence, the step 0.4 label table and readings 1 and 3-6 are unchanged from r9. The step 0.4 forecast and the new consistency checks are reported only.

packed.verdict: r10 resolves 10 of the 11 r9 digest items in the text itself, not just in the Review 10 table, and implements user decisions (a) and (b) correctly and consistently. Reading 2 condition (b) appears identically at Part 2 lines 216-219, V0(d) line 678, reading 2 lines 714-717, the Part 5 consistency check at 702 and Part 8.2(iii) lines 873-874. K1c's relative clause takes both medians over the C-valid anchors at lines 226, 655 and 686 and in Part 8.2(iv). The dominance proof that the gate now covers the relative clause holds: C-valid median M >= 0.65 and M - 0.15 >= 0.5M. Neither decision opens a false-PASS path. Condition (b) only withholds a reading. Decision (b) changes which anchors the relative clause uses, and item 5's 90% rule limits how many anchors can be dropped. I found no other change to a gate, label, precedence or approval rule. Every example recomputes. The 47-anchor case gives 0.9/0.9/0/0.45, and 0.90 with positive KC_R zeroed. The 48-anchor case gives 0.60/0.60/0/0.70, share 23/25 and median KC_C 0.70. The K1c case gives 0.66, 0.70, C-valid KC 1.40 and the alternative bar 0.33. All 38 Part 11 hashes match. The one item resolved only in part is #11, the 4.8 batching. The protocol fixes the batch but treats the same batch as enough to guarantee bit-identical float32 actor outputs. It drops the digest's 'same jit' and does not pin the runtime stack under which rerun1 reproduced 143/143 contexts byte-identically. It also leaves the identical 1e-9 tension at the 4.5 cross-check untouched. The remaining issues are small: a per-cell vs per-bank wording slip, the step 0.4 forecast's base set, and Review 10 bookkeeping. One more text-only pass would close them, and none affects a gate's logic.

low_findings.section: 4.5 Independent Q^pi evaluator (line 385) vs 4.8 batching rationale (line 472)
low_findings.claim: r10's own rationale says a Q^pi row compounds up to 100 actor calls, so batching must be fixed for a 1e-9 comparison. The same reasoning applies to the 4.5 cross-check, which compares a new raw dynamics() loop with the environment-based evaluator at 1e-9 relative across all three worlds. r10 says nothing there about matching the actor batching. A different batch (for example one row at a time in the raw loop) can produce float32 actions that differ by a ULP and fail the check with no real fault.
low_findings.evidence: Line 385: 'checked against the environment-based evaluator at every step 0.4 anchor, at three slots ..., in all three worlds, to 1e-9 relative'. Step 0.4 label table line 606: 'evaluator cross-check fails' -> INCOMPLETE. The step 0.4 continuations are the frozen actors, clipped (line 592). Clipping removes differences only where the action saturates.
low_findings.fix: Add to 4.5: 'both evaluators obtain each actor action from the same call with the same batch and row order, or the second evaluator consumes the first evaluator's recorded float32 actions'. Alternatively, state why 1e-9 holds there.

low_findings.claim: 'called once per cell with all 32 anchors at evaluation.py line 437' and 'one call per time offset on ... all 32 x 6 anchor-slot pairs of a cell' are imprecise. A cell has two banks (ordinary and strong_current), so continuation_values runs twice per cell, once per bank with 32 anchors. A literal reading, one call per cell, would batch 64 anchors, which continuation_values accepts (n <= 64) but which would not match the recorded batch. Also, offset 0 makes no actor call: the first action comes from the bank.
low_findings.evidence: There are 18 files matching run/evaluation/*__native__20000__*.json for the 'nine cells' of line 464, each with per_probe qpi of shape (32, 6). evaluate_snapshot is called per bank (evaluate_worker.py:604; out['context']=bank['context'], evaluation.py:421). reference.py:254 requires 1 <= n <= 64. reference.py:265-269 uses first[active] at offset 0 and actor_actions only for offset >= 1.
low_findings.fix: Reword as 'one call per offset >= 1 on the active rows of the 32 x 6 anchor-slot pairs of one cell and bank (context), in the original row order; continuation_values is called once per cell and bank, 18 calls in all'. Align Review 10 row 11.

verified.section: 4.8 Q^pi reproduction, Batching bullet (line 472); r9 digest item 11; Review 10 row 11 (line 1163)
verified.claim: The bullet says that because 'each actor call then sees the same batch as the recorded one, ... the float32 actions repeat, and 1e-9 absorbs only float64 summation order'. A matching batch is necessary for bit-identical GPU float32 outputs but not sufficient. The r9 digest's fix also asked for the 'same jit', which r10 dropped, and the protocol does not pin the stack under which the saved values were produced.
verified.evidence: Saved values came from a GPU, jit, float32 runtime pinned at rerun1 runtime.py:51-59: jax/jaxlib 0.6.2, cuda12 plugin, backend 'gpu', jax_default_matmul_precision == 'highest'. The actor was compiled as jax.jit(lambda obs: actor.apply_fn(...).sample(seed=None)) at evaluate_worker.py:351. DRAFT_PROTOCOL.md mentions none of 'highest', 0.6.2 or the device kind (grep). The protocol itself expects GPU nondeterminism (lines 494, 498-499). One float32 ULP is 1.19e-7 relative (scratch examples.py), so a single differing action in up to 100 compounding calls can exceed 1e-9. The mismatch is then INCOMPLETE, and a repeat under unchanged code ends the step INCONCLUSIVE (line 498), which stops the line of work with no real fault. There is empirical support the draft does not cite: rerun1 RUN_RESULT.json reproduction gives tier1_exact = 143 and largest_tier2_scaled_deviation = 0.0, so the same stack and batching did reproduce bit for bit.
verified.fix: Require the 4.8 reproduction to run the actor through the same compiled function on the rerun1 stack: same jax/jaxlib/CUDA plugin versions, GPU device kind, matmul precision 'highest', same batch and row order. Cite rerun1 RUN_RESULT.json (143/143 Tier-1 byte-identical) as the evidence for bit-identity. Replace 'so the float32 actions repeat' with 'so, on the same stack, the float32 actions are expected to repeat bit for bit (rerun1 evidence)'.

check.reason: Confirmed as written. DRAFT_PROTOCOL.md:472 pins the batch and row order and then concludes 'so the float32 actions repeat'. Nothing in the draft pins the stack or the compiled function the new evaluator must use: a grep finds no 'highest', no 0.6.2, no device kind, no jit or FrozenPolicy requirement. Line 399 says only that 'the new evaluator' does the 4.8 reproduction. The r9 digest fix (VERIFY_CRITIC_DIGEST_r9.txt:61) asked for 'same jit', and Review 10 row 11 (:1163) drops it. The recorded values came from FrozenPolicy._act = jax.jit(lambda obs: actor.apply_fn(...).sample(seed=None)) (evaluate_worker.py:351), called through reference.actor_actions -> policy.act (reference.py:115-130) inside continuation_values (reference.py:259-272). That ran under runtime_receipt's pins (rerun1 runtime.py:51-59: jax/jaxlib/cuda12 0.6.2, backend gpu, float32, matmul precision 'highest'). A matching batch shape does not by itself give bit-identical float32 outputs if the evaluator jits differently (fusion into a larger jit, a different precision flag or a different device), and one ULP drift compounding over up to 100 calls exceeds 1e-9. The stated rationale therefore overclaims, and the fix is incomplete. The evidence the finding cites exists: rerun1 RUN_RESULT.json reproduction.tier1_exact = 143, tier2_near_exact = 0, largest_tier2_scaled_deviation = 0.0. That shows bit-identity on the same stack, and the draft does not cite it. Severity is lowered from medium to low. The failure is fail-closed: a mismatch is INCOMPLETE (:472), never a false PASS or a wrong reading. After a first INCOMPLETE, the 5.0 rules (:495-497) allow one code-only fix before the rerun, such as switching to the rerun1 compiled path, so INCONCLUSIVE follows only if the cause is not diagnosed. The cost is an extra A2 cycle, which is the same Low class the r9 round gave this item (R9-7 / digest item 11). The suggested fix is still right: require the same compiled actor function on the rerun1 runtime (the runtime_receipt pins plus the same batch and row order), cite RUN_RESULT.json 143/143 Tier-1, and qualify 'repeat' as 'expected to repeat bit for bit on the same stack'. Both parts of the fix are text-only and change no gate.

The result would be INCOMPLETE and possibly INCONCLUSIVE. It can never produce a false pass.

Any reachability miss voids the whole stage (the user kept this scoping), and RANDOM's kink rounding or noise within V0(b)'s band can cause that miss.

No power estimate exists. Six criteria and five V0 items must hold in each of three seeds, and noise in either critic's KC (never measured on the new critics) can turn a true effect into FAIL-mixed or INCONCLUSIVE.

K1c's absolute clause has no designed margin at the gate edge. A CUTOFF critic that is correct on average but noisy can FAIL K1c and receive reading 1 ('does not over-value'), and the protocol does not flag that case.
The K1a companions (low-gap share, median KC_C alone) and the zeroed-K1a value are reported only. A K1a pass carried by low-gap anchors where RANDOM under-values is disclosed, not blocked.

Learner competence and reach remain the open empirical risks. The Stage 1 continuations may produce smaller gaps than the reference continuations used in the step 0.4 forecast, and the step 0.4 forecast counts invalid anchors more pessimistically than Stage 1 does.
